# x402socks.com — SOCKS5 and HTTP CONNECT proxy for AI agents

## What this service is

x402socks.com is a **proxy service**. When you route a request through an exit
node, the destination server sees a connection coming from that exit node
instead of from your own network — that is what a forward proxy does.

The product is **instant access and fast, well-placed exit nodes**: pick a
region, pay, connect, start working within seconds, without an account, an
email address, or a sales call.

**Anonymity and privacy are secondary effects, not the product.** The service
is not an anonymity network, not a VPN, and not an identity-hiding system. It
does not change your origin payload, does not make you indistinguishable from
other users of the same exit, and does not promise that the destination cannot
correlate or identify you by other means (cookies, logins, fingerprinting,
payload content, your own client behaviour). If a task needs strong anonymity,
this service is not the right tool. If a task needs a fast, reliable,
region-selectable egress hop that an automated client can drive, it is.

Access and performance are provided on a **best-effort** basis. Availability,
throughput, compatibility, and fitness for a particular purpose are not
guaranteed. Failed connections are non-refundable by default; repeated or
systemic failures from the same customer may be reviewed manually after contact
via Telegram: https://t.me/x402socks

## Protocols — every exit speaks all three

Every exit node serves the **same three dialects on the same token, the same
entitlements, and the same accounting**. There is no preferred protocol, no
second-class exit, and no plan to retire any of them.

| Dialect | Port | Proxy URL | Use it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SOCKS5** (RFC 1928) | TCP **1080** | `socks5h://exit:1080` | Default. Best choice for automation: `curl`, Go/Python/Node proxy clients, headless browsers via a forwarder, SSH `ProxyCommand`, anything that can send credentials. |
| **HTTP CONNECT** | TCP **3128** | `http://exit:3128` | Plaintext HTTP proxy hop. Works with clients that only understand `http://` proxies and with browsers that prompt for proxy credentials. |
| **HTTP CONNECT over TLS** | TCP **3129** | `https://exit:3129` | Same adapter over TLS. Use for Chrome/Chromium-based tools and any client where the client-to-node hop should be encrypted. |

Both CONNECT dialects tunnel **both** kinds of origin: an `https://` target
(TLS to the destination, verified end-to-end by your client) and a plain
`http://` target. The proxy port selects the hop dialect; the target scheme is
independent and is carried inside the CONNECT request.

The port and the dialect are fixed pairs. `http://exit:3128` and
`https://exit:3129` both answer `407 Proxy Authentication Required` when
unauthenticated. `https://exit:3128` is not a TLS listener — connecting with TLS
to it stalls until the client times out — and `http://exit:3129` aborts because
that listener expects a TLS handshake. Set the proxy scheme and port to match
the table, and do not probe ports.

All eight exits expose `1080`, `3128`, and `3129`:

- `us-west1` — US California
- `us-central1` — US Texas
- `us-east1` — US New York
- `us-north1` — US Northwest
- `eu-central1` — EU Paris
- `eu-north1` — EU Riga
- `asia-central1` — ASIA Singapore
- `asia-west1` — ASIA India

Last wire check (2026-11-20): all 24 port probes open, all eight `:3129`
listeners present a valid certificate for their own hostname, all eight `:3128`
listeners answer `407` to an unauthenticated CONNECT, all eight `:3129`
listeners answer `407` over TLS, and all eight `:1080` listeners require
authentication. Treat this as a snapshot; `GET /nodes.json` plus a single
handshake is the live check.

`GET /nodes.json` (or `https://api.x402socks.com/api/v1/nodes`) is the
authoritative live list: hostname, port, region, coordinates, health, and a
`disabled` marker. Do not hardcode the table above as a capability claim; read
the feed. A `disabled: true` or non-healthy node should be skipped, not retried.

### Dialect differences that matter

- SOCKS5 carries the token as username **and** password (RFC 1929). It is
  application-agnostic and works for both TCP and DNS-at-exit (`socks5h`).
- HTTP CONNECT carries the token in `Proxy-Authorization: Basic ...` (token as
  both user and password), or via the client's proxy credential prompt.
  Unauthenticated requests get `407 Proxy Authentication Required`.
- Plaintext `:3128` exposes the CONNECT target and the token on the
  client-to-node hop. That is a property of plaintext HTTP proxying, not a
  warning that the port is going away — if that exposure matters for your
  workload, use `:3129` or SOCKS5 instead.
- TLS on `:3129` protects the **client-to-exit hop only**. It does not encrypt
  the origin payload, does not protect the exit node itself, and does not
  rescue a token that leaked on your side. Certificates are issued per
  hostname, so **always address the exit by hostname, never by IP**, or
  verification fails.

There is no protocol negotiation, upgrade path, or capability probing: connect
to the port that matches the dialect your client speaks.

## Authentication

Proxy access requires a token obtained through x402 or a direct payment.

```sh
# SOCKS5 (recommended default)
curl --proxy socks5h://us-central1.x402socks.com:1080 \
  --proxy-user "$TOKEN:$TOKEN" https://api.example.com

# HTTP CONNECT
curl --proxy http://us-central1.x402socks.com:3128 \
  --proxy-user "$TOKEN:$TOKEN" https://api.example.com

# HTTP CONNECT over TLS
curl --proxy https://us-central1.x402socks.com:3129 \
  --proxy-user "$TOKEN:$TOKEN" https://api.example.com
```

The examples substitute `$TOKEN` from your environment. **Never** put a token
in a URL, in source control, in browser storage, in logs, in analytics, in
screenshots, or in shell history. Treat it exactly like a password: anyone
holding it can spend the plan's remaining time and traffic.

Check the account behind a token:

- `POST /api/token/status` — status, expiry, usage
- `POST /api/token/validate` — `204` when valid

## Connecting Chrome and Chromium-based tools

Chrome cannot ask for SOCKS5 credentials itself (it delegates that prompt to
the OS, which has none), so plain SOCKS5 is not directly usable from Chrome's
proxy settings. Use CONNECT — TLS is available on **every** exit, so there is
no exit you have to avoid:

```sh
# TLS HTTP proxy (preferred for headless Chrome/Chromium, Playwright, Puppeteer, Selenium)
--proxy-server=https://us-central1.x402socks.com:3129

# PAC entry
HTTPS us-central1.x402socks.com:3129

# Plaintext HTTP proxy, if the tooling only supports http://
--proxy-server=http://us-central1.x402socks.com:3128
```

On the first request Chrome shows its built-in proxy credential dialog after
`407`; enter the token as **both** username and password. PAC files and manual
proxy settings behave the same way. Firefox supports an HTTPS proxy natively
(Settings → Network Settings → Manual proxy configuration, plus "Also use this
proxy for HTTPS").

For headless automation that needs an encrypted hop, use `:3129`. For anything
that speaks SOCKS5 natively, `:1080` is the simplest path.

## Rapid reconnection and back-off

Closing a tunnel and immediately reconnecting can be refused while the prior
session drains: HTTP CONNECT answers `407 Proxy Authentication Required` and
SOCKS5 reports an authentication rejection. This affects all three dialects on
all exits and is deliberate back-off for flapping clients, **not** a credential
problem.

Wait about a second, then back off exponentially (1s, 2s, 4s, capped). Do not
rotate the token, buy again, or disable authentication because of it. If
refusals persist after backed-off retries, check `GET /nodes.json` and the
account state instead of retrying harder.

## Payment

Two rails, same catalog:

**x402 (recommended for agents).** `POST https://payments.x402socks.com/v1/access/{package_id}`
with an empty JSON body (`{}`). The first response is `402` with a
`PAYMENT-REQUIRED` header. Select the exact requirement advertised there, sign
an x402 v2 EIP-3009 authorization, and retry with `PAYMENT-SIGNATURE`.

Runtime challenge fields are authoritative. Never invent an amount, recipient,
token contract, or network from documentation — including this file.

As of the last check (2026-11-20), the challenge advertises Base mainnet USDC
(`eip155:8453`, asset `0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913`, recipient
`0x73BAE3c48d34d71C4CEa76DFdaa3bE2cF4d335a1`) with a 300 s window and an atomic
amount of `1000000`. Re-read the challenge at call time; it can change.

**Direct checkout (humans).** https://x402socks.com/buy supports the configured
direct rails — Ethereum USDC/USDT, Base USDC, and BNB Smart Chain USDC/USDT. It
creates a payment intent and issues a one-time token once the exact on-chain
transfer is confirmed.

A broadcast transfer may wait for confirmations; the service retries
confirmation and the checkout keeps polling. **Never send a second transfer for
the same intent.** If the payment window elapses before confirmation, the intent
closes and is not completed automatically — keep the transaction hash and ask
in the Telegram channel rather than paying twice.

## Packages

Read `GET /catalog.json` (`/packages.json` and `/prices.json` are aliases;
`https://api.x402socks.com/api/v1/packages` is the authoritative API route) for
the live catalog, prices, and entitlements. Last observed set:

| id | name | price (USD) | entitlement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `time_6h` | 6 Hours | $1.00 | 6 h, up to 1 GB, 1 session |
| `time_1d` | 1 Day | $3.59 | 24 h, up to 10 GB, 1 session |
| `time_7d` | 7 Days | $9.99 | 7 days, up to 75 GB, 1 session |
| `usage_5gb` | 5 GB | $6.99 | 5 GB, no time limit, 1 session |
| `usage_50gb` | 50 GB | $34.99 | 50 GB, no time limit, 1 session |
| `multi_agent` | Multi-Agent Month | $29.99 | 30 days, up to 300 GB, up to 5 sessions |

This table is a snapshot for orientation. `catalog.json` is the contract;
prices and fair-use limits change there first.

## Credential recovery

If an x402 payment settled but the issued token was lost, recover it with the
paying wallet instead of paying again. Recovery never charges.

```http
POST https://payments.x402socks.com/v1/access/recover
Content-Type: application/json

{"transaction":"0xSETTLEMENT_TX_HASH","signature":"0xEIP191_SIGNATURE","issued_at":1792000000}
```

`signature` is a `0x`-hex EIP-191 signature (`personal_sign` / `signMessage`)
from the wallet that settled the payment, over exactly these UTF-8 bytes with no
trailing newline:

```
x402socks credential recovery v1
tx_hash: 0xSETTLEMENT_TX_HASH
issued_at: 1792000000
```

`issued_at` must be within ±10 minutes of the current time, so a captured
signature cannot be replayed later. Success returns the account and a fresh
token that replaces the lost one.

Errors: `400` `invalid_request` / `stale_recovery` / `invalid_signature`;
`403` `ownership_not_proven` (the signature does not recover to the paying
wallet — the original `PAYMENT-SIGNATURE` is rejected here deliberately, since
settlement calldata is public and replayable); `404` `not_recoverable`;
`409` `account_inactive`; `410` `plan_expired` (fail-closed, no automatic
catch-up); `502` `recovery_unavailable` (safe to retry later).

The route is rate-limited and intentionally absent from `openapi.json` because
it is not payable.

## Token rotation

A client that still holds a valid token can roll it without support:

```http
POST https://api.x402socks.com/api/v1/token/rotate
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN
```

Success returns `200 {"account":{...},"token":"NEW_TOKEN"}`. The presented token
stops working immediately for the proxy and for every route, so move all your
clients to the new value at once. Unknown, inactive, or expired tokens get
`401 "a valid token is required"` and nothing changes. Rotations are recorded on
the account as `account.token_rotated` with `source self-service`. Rotate on
suspicion of exposure; if the token is already gone, use recovery instead.

## Discovery surfaces

- `/llms.txt` — this file; the agent-facing contract
- `/.well-known/x402` — x402 payment metadata (network, asset, recipient, exits)
- `/catalog.json`, `/packages.json`, `/prices.json` — public catalog
- `/nodes.json` — exit feed with health and `disabled` markers
- `/api/health`, `/api/nodes`, `/api/token/status`, `/api/token/validate`
- `/faq`, `/status` — human help and reachability status
- `https://payments.x402socks.com/openapi.json` — OpenAPI 3.1.0 for payable resources
- `https://api.x402socks.com/api/v1/packages` — authoritative package/pricing API

`/api/v1/` is the versioned namespace: additive fields are compatible, breaking
changes ship under a new version with a changelog entry. Protocol ports,
credentials, and the token contract are stable — no dialect is scheduled for
removal.

## Evidence boundaries

`/status`, health endpoints, node reachability, TCP port checks, and a `402`
challenge prove **only** reachability and that a payment is requested. They do
not prove settlement, account provisioning, usage accounting, expiry
enforcement, restart durability, or isolation between accounts. Claims about
those behaviours require authenticated, funded evidence — do not infer them
from an unauthenticated probe.

## Agent skill

The companion skill is published at
[github.com/X402Socks/skill](https://github.com/X402Socks/skill) and listed at
[skills.sh/X402Socks/skill](https://skills.sh/X402Socks/skill). It wraps the
purchase loop: quote a job, pay on Base via x402, receive a token, route through
the exit pool, and verify status — referencing this document rather than
duplicating the payment and token contracts.

```bash
npx skills add X402Socks/skill
# or
git clone https://github.com/X402Socks/skill
```

## Support

Telegram: https://t.me/x402socks — overpayments, uncertain payments, expired
intents, and account issues are resolved manually and audited. There is no
automatic refund or retry path; contact support with your transaction hash
instead of paying again.
